summary:
Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women. The offence covers sodomy and, per the Human Dignity Trust country profile, acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent, so conduct short of intercourse can still fall within the criminal law.

Amnesty International's report of 9 January 2024 (index AFR 01/7533/2024), 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries', documents rising anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people in the countries it examines, including Zimbabwe. The report's finding of law being used as an instrument of hostility is the operative risk context for a visitor, alongside the statutory exposure itself.

Healthcare access is formally protected. In July 2018 Zimbabwe's health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gay people, sex workers and transgender and gender-non-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states that care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty, noting that nowhere in policy or law does it say it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups. It was issued precisely because patients had avoided clinics for fear of mistreatment or of staff tipping off police. A trans visitor can therefore expect public facilities to be formally obliged to treat them, while day-to-day treatment still depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Support infrastructure exists despite criminalisation. GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe), a voluntary membership organisation established in 1990, reports more than 4,000 community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups and 4 resource centres. Its services include legal support explicitly covering 'sodomy' arrests, counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes. Legal aid and counselling are reachable for a traveller who needs assistance.

Social hostility, rather than routine prosecution, is the more likely pressure a visitor encounters. Academic work on Zimbabwean social work describes homosexuals living secluded lives because of prejudice, which points to concealment as the ordinary survival strategy and to exposure in public as the trigger for trouble.
tangentialFactors:
Academic literature on Zimbabwe frames same-sex relations as indigenous rather than imported, with Mabvurira et al. (International Journal of Humanities and Social Science, July 2012) arguing that homosexuality is 'as African as the baobab tree and as Zimbabwean as the Great Zimbabwe Ruins' and tracing same-sex relations in pre-colonial and post-colonial Zimbabwe. The same paper calls on social workers to promote social justice for the gay community, indicating an organised professional constituency arguing against stigma.

The 2018 health handbook is a policy instrument rather than a statute, and it addresses service delivery rather than decriminalisation; the criminal provisions and the healthcare guarantee operate simultaneously and do not offset one another.
localsOnly:
GALZ has operated since 1990 and reports 4,000-plus community members organised through 10 affinity groups across 4 resource centres, with legal support, counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes available to LGBTI Zimbabweans.

Health practitioners in public institutions are trained under a 68-page ministry handbook covering gays, sex workers and transgender or gender-non-conforming patients, which states that providing care to these groups is legal and every provider's duty.

Residents face the same criminal provisions covering sodomy and indecent contact between males, and prejudice documented in social work research pushes much of the community into concealed, secluded living.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the penalties attached to the sodomy and indecency offences, so the severity of exposure on conviction is unresolved here.

Whether Zimbabwe provides legal gender recognition, and on what terms a trans person can change identity documents, is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved.

The frequency and pattern of prosecutions under the sodomy provisions, and whether the 2024 Amnesty International findings have produced specific enforcement actions in Zimbabwe, are not established by these sources.

It is unresolved whether the 2018 health ministry handbook remains in force, has been revised, or is applied uniformly across public facilities; only its July 2018 release is documented.
